column1: # Book 4 second-round read (Fable, 2026-10-30): every line read against the Latin. No changes.
# 4.638 itaque presents the snake as a consequence, not a ground.
# 4.766-767 memory fails to object that the man is long dead; "is not the one" had denied the identity the Latin asserts.

column2: and so there is a snake which, touched by a man's spittle,
and does not protest that this one is in the grip of death and doom
long since, whom the mind believes it sees alive.

column1: # 4.734 note: 1.135 reads "morte obita quorum tellus amplectitur ossa"; the words are the same, the order differs.
# 4.776 note: particulae also occurs at 4.261, 3.665, 3.708 and 2.833; "here only" was false.

column2: whose bones, after death, the earth embraces; {{NOTE: repeats 1.135 in the Latin with the words reordered; the English repeats its own line}}
the abundance of tiny parts, that it can supply them. {{NOTE: particulae, Lucretius's diminutive, as at 4.261 and in Book 3; the tiny parts are the images themselves, not the first-beginnings}}
